extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of drama, playwrights, and literary/theatre scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing tragic plots, characters, and theatrical structure according to Aristotle's Poetics (how to produce effective tragedy that evokes pity and fear).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry generalizes; history particularizes
rubrics_metrics.description: “For it generalizes rather, whereas history particularizes.” Fiction (poetry) formulates principles and types (combinations of qualities and circumstances) rather than registering particular facts as history does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat fiction as the study of types and principles: invent or combine characteristic features to illustrate general truths rather than merely recording particulars. Use characters as embodiments of qualities to explore general human possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use elimination, combination, and aesthetic complement in character-construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The main differences between history and fiction are analysed as elimination, combination and aesthetic complement: the last being a principle by which two or more attractions combined give greater pleasure than the separate values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose characters and incidents by selecting salient features (elimination), combining traits from different sources (combination), and arranging elements so their combination yields greater aesthetic pleasure (aesthetic complement). Avoid reproducing every factual detail of originals—select features that serve the principle you wish to exhibit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis) as a source of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: “The characteristic offers the subject ... specially favourable conditions for recognition. In part lies its importance as a source of pleasure. For to make out and to recognize is to judge. If the judgment takes place with special ease, precision and certainty, the act is accompanied by pleasure, supposing always that such a judgment is not too commonplace or trivial.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design moments of recognition so that the audience can make the cognitive leap with satisfying clarity (not too obvious, not trivial). Recognition should reward the audience's reasoning capacities and produce pleasure alongside emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of names (historical vs casual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy often uses epithets or stock names; Tragedy adheres to historical names because the potential is a matter of faith and a familiar name ‘implies a crowd of situations.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose names according to genre and the audience's presumed knowledge: use known/historical names in tragedy when you rely on the audience's assumed acquaintance; use epithets or stock names in comedy. Beware inventing or altering well-known narratives in ways that violate audience expectations about key facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select plausible subject matter within audience belief
rubrics_metrics.description: The field of poetry is the potential or possible; one must choose subjects the audience will accept as possible. Stories that are neither extremely ancient nor quite modern are most agreeable: the ancient may be disbelieved, the very modern may be too near to take pleasure in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick subjects and setting that fall within the audience’s range of believable possibility. Avoid extremes of remoteness or immediate contemporaneity that undercut the audience’s willingness to engage imaginatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible liberties in detail—preserve salient features
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberties in matters of detail will not be resented provided the salient features of the story are not violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may alter incidental facts, but preserve the core elements of familiar tales (the salient features) so the audience is not left uncertain about what is true or essential. Skilled invention should respect those elements the audience counts as central.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot complexity and causal necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are simple or complex. A complex plot involves a Disclosure, the Irony of Fate, or both, and these ought to be deduced from the original structure of the story so their occurrence comes about from the antecedents by law of nature or moral certainty; there is a vast difference between sequel and consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make reversals and recognitions arise plausibly from prior causes (natural law or moral probability) so the plot’s developments feel necessary or highly probable rather than arbitrary sequels. Favor complex plots (with reversal/recognition) when they can be logically grounded in antecedent facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine Irony of Fate and Recognition for maximum effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The finest form of Disclosure of Mistaken Identity is one accompanied by the Irony of Fate; such a combination will be either piteous or terrible and is the imaginative experience which Tragedy most portrays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for scenarios where recognition (anagnorisis) and ironic reversal (peripeteia) interact so that the outcome both surprises and feels inevitable—this combination produces the strongest tragic emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure (anagnorisis) — transform stranger into acquaintance
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of Mistaken Identity is the transformation of the doomed or elect of the play from being strangers into acquaintances; the story will be more seriously affected by the disclosure of the identity of the main characters than by any other sort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use identification revelations that reframe relationships between characters (e.g., parent/child, kin) because these yield stronger moral and emotional consequences than trivial disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catastrophe defined (physical or moral destruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Catastrophe is an experience involving destruction or pain, e.g. physical death, a broken heart, mutilation, etc.; often what befalls the hero is moral rather than physical death (disgrace, calamity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the catastrophe meaningful: it can be literal death or a moral/social ruin that renders life unbearable. Design catastrophes as integral outcomes of the plot’s causal chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural components of tragedy: prologue, scene, finale, chorus
rubrics_metrics.description: The anatomical divisions of a Tragedy are Prologue (all that comes before the Introit of the Chorus), Scene (between choric odes), Finale (followed by no choric ode); the Chorus includes Introit, Stationary (a choric ode not in anapaests or trochees), and Lamentation (a plaintive song involving both actors and chorus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize the play into these structural parts and use choric odes, lamentation and other choric functions where appropriate to the type. Understand each part’s role in pacing, exposition, and emotional modulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy’s emotional aim: portray the terrible and the piteous
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of the ideal tragedy should be complex and it should portray the terrible and piteous—this being the peculiarity of this kind of fiction; every tragedy must counterfeit the terrible and the piteous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center the play on incidents and character developments that elicit pity and fear. Avoid diverting Tragedy to effects that belong to other genres (e.g., mere sensationalism or comedy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic hero’s moral mean: neither perfect nor thoroughly wicked
rubrics_metrics.description: The virtuous ought not be represented in transition from good to ill fortune, nor the thoroughly wicked in transition from ill to good. The tragic hero should be the mean: neither a paragon of virtue nor morally depraved, but someone of high status who errs seriously (by mistake) and falls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a hero of high rank/quality who commits an error (hamartia) rather than deliberate vice; this ensures pity (unmerited misfortune) and fear (what might happen to someone like ourselves). Avoid heroes who are entirely flawless or wholly villainous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity (singleness) of action
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constructed story must be single rather than double; its transition should be from good to ill and occasioned by some serious error, not wickedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain focus on one main action or causal chain rather than two parallel, contrasting fates. Keep the plot unified so emotional energy concentrates on the central tragic reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke pity and fear through the story, not spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Alarm and tears may be evoked by the exhibition (spectacle), but they can also be by the story, and this is most natural and more artistic. It is less expensive and more artistic to produce the effect by the plot than by properties; those who produce the monstrous by properties have nothing in common with Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on well-constructed plot and character to produce emotional responses; avoid cheap sensationalism or overreliance on stagecraft to create effects appropriate to Tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use familial/close relations for tragic coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: Such experiences must be shared by connexions, enemies or neutrals. A man earns no tears by killing an enemy or a neutral, but when catastrophes occur between persons who belong to each other (brothers, parent and child, etc.) these aspects should be sought for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft tragedies around relationships of kinship or close connection to maximize pity. Avoid structuring catastrophic events that primarily affect strangers, which elicit less pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect traditional narratives; invent skilfully
rubrics_metrics.description: You may not violate traditional narratives (e.g., the murder of Clytaemnestra by Orestes); you should invent yourself and make skilful use of the tradition. Alteration of a vital part in a familiar narrative will be resented by the spectator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If adapting or drawing on well-known stories, preserve the narrative’s essential elements; introduce innovation where it does not betray central, familiar truths. Skillful invention supplements tradition rather than undermines it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graded types of intentionality in atrocity (ranking of outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternatives for the agent: perpetrate or not, and consciously or not. The worst is conscious projection without perpetration (shocks without tears); next worst is conscious projection with perpetration; better is unconscious projection with perpetration followed by disclosure; best is discovering identity in time (meaning to kill but prevented by recognition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer plots where the atrocity is either unwittingly committed with later disclosure (to produce pity and terror) or where recognition prevents the atrocity at the last moment. Avoid relying on mere conscious intent without consequent catastrophe, which shocks but fails to move.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character delineation — aim for goodness
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the four things to aim at in the delineation of character, the first and most important is that the characters should be good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select characters with qualities that invite audience sympathy; a wholly villainous cast undermines the production of pity and tragic interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character delineation — appropriateness (to species/status)
rubrics_metrics.description: The second point is that character should be appropriate: it is possible for a person to be brave, yet for the species of courage to be unsuitable if the person be a woman (or belong to an inappropriate class).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure virtues and behaviors suit the character’s social role, gender expectations, and status as understood by the audience; incongruous traits reduce credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character delineation — likeness (probable/typical)
rubrics_metrics.description: The third is that character should be like (i.e., plausible or typical), distinct from merely being good or appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray characters who act in ways consistent with their portrayed nature and with human psychology so the audience recognizes them as believable types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character delineation — psychological expression through speech and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech or Conduct will be psychological if it reveals any intention with which a course is adopted or rejected; the character delineated will be good if the intention be so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dialogue and visible actions to disclose characters’ intentions and moral makeup. Characterization must be shown through intentional behavior rather than merely narrated.
